<!-- # The Math And The Type Theory -->

## An Extended Abstract

<p align="left"><em>Know yourself and know your enemy, and you will not worry about the results of a hundred battles.</em></p>
<p style="text-align:right;">Sun Tzu</p>

[Last time](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/LqsctjJbk5HHPD4Jm/the-math-and-the-territory-1), we went over an overview of a certain relationship between mathematics and the real world (the world we care about). This was, in a sense, summarized by the diagram below:

![][image1]

To progress into a conceptual framework (framing, language) of what it means when the math matches the territory and what tools we can develop through said framework to identify material mismatches between the math and the territory, we have reduced the dimension of the problem to one illustrated by the following diagram:

![][image2]

Here we illustrate the action of formalizing/representing mathematics as a particular type theory. It has been established that type theory can be used as a foundation of mathematics. The two diagrams encode a similar shape of relationship between one thing and another thing used in the “representation” of the former thing.

The argument we present is that certain type theories are not sufficient to represent particular mathematical concepts faithfully. Therefore, we pose the question of whether there exists a type theory that can faithfully represent mathematics as we humans “know it” or “as mathematicians do it”. [Vladimir Voevodsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Voevodsky) was certainly worried about this, and he developed a foundation of mathematics that would allow the faithful[^1] representation of mathematics.

We then hope to lift the argument into the question of “The Math and The Territory”.

# Type Theory

In recent years, interest in formalizing mathematics in computer systems has significantly increased. The [Lean](https://lean-lang.org/) project is leading this charge and has had a lot of success in building a “digital” foundation of [mathematics](https://mathlib-initiative.org/). Much of the technical chops of Lean (the language) as a foundation of mathematics can be attributed to it being based on type theory, in particular, [Dependent Type Theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dependent+type+theory).[^2] 

In general, type theory can be seen as a branch of mathematics that, as we have seen above, can be used to formalize mathematical concepts. There are many “flavours” of type theories, each with certain features that make it suitable to express classes of mathematical concepts; it is through this diversity of type theories that we observe that some of them can be more effective in expressing complex mathematics than others. Other than the matter of complexity, we also want the type theory to “do” mathematics in the same way that we do and understand mathematics. This is often a matter of taste and pedantry. The latter of which has led to a sprawl of type theories. We are not considering the implementation of type theories, as they can also be a source of contention regarding faithfulness between the theoretical type theory and the implemented type theory. Although it is through these implementations that we get a sense of the formalization ability of the various type theories. It doesn’t help that implementations of type theories are also general-purpose programming languages. This lends certain “programming tricks” to be used when formalizing mathematical concepts that may not be available in the conceptual type theory. A good example of this difference can be observed in [Book HoTT](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Book+HoTT) vs particular implementations of Homotopy Type Theory, say [cubical-agda](https://agda.readthedocs.io/en/latest/language/cubical.html) (which makes use of [cubical type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cubical%2Btype%2Btheory)) or Coq. Mathematicians working in these systems always cite tricks or in-group esoteric knowledge of why a particular formalization is actually the correct way to do it. Or, in other cases, not the correct way to do it. Given that most of this is anecdotal, evidence of this is either found in forums such as Zulip or obscure Discord channels, talks and presentations, and conversations. 

This points to the crux of our argument: new type theories are invented/discovered because existing type theories are not sufficient to express what mathematicians find relevant. Granted that most research on type theories is done by “foundationalists” and not necessarily “real mathematicians”, what they find relevant as “a certain kind of mathematician” may not be the same as what a “real mathematician” might care about. That said, we are going to assume that the type theorists are real mathematicians.

The observation that led us to this was: there seem to be many languages of formal mathematics and many type theories for the same. Why can’t we have one type theory to “rule them all”? I suppose this is what [Narya](https://narya.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) is hinting at, with it being “a step below the [one ring](https://lotr.fandom.com/wiki/One_Ring)”.

## When is a Type Theory Insufficient

I suppose it is a hobby for some category theorists and type theorists to invent new type theories over the weekend; this is a sense I get when going through research in type theory. To me, this points to an inadequacy/insufficiency of existing type theories in expressing what the mathematicians are interested in. I’m not alone in this, as some mathematical philosophers have also expressed this sense.[^3][^4]

This also happens with programming languages, mathematics, and natural language. In the case of mathematics, new fields of the subject are born out of the need for new ways to express certain ideas that were not possible using the existing mathematical structures. These new mathematical frameworks also lead to breakthroughs in the way we understand the world and what we can build (engineering applications). A good example of this is the “invention” of [calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus), which led to Newtonian mechanics and is widely used today in the design [of spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft).

In a way, inventing new type systems helps us see the world of mathematics better. It also allows us to computationally express ideas that we couldn’t express previously via other type theories. Much of the formalization revolution we are currently witnessing in maths is due to the invention of dependent types. We are going to show how one type theory fails to express a certain mathematical concept and how, by introducing another type theory, we are able to express the same mathematical concept.

An obvious example of this is in [CCHM](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.02108); the “new” cubical type theory allows us to prove and use univalence computationally. This is in contrast with Book HoTT, where univalence is stated as an axiom. This additional expressivity was not possible until cubical sets came into the picture.

We go over more examples of when different foundations and type theories fail and how introducing other foundations resolves the failures.

### Axiom of Choice

A rather simple (cop out) example is that of the axiom of choice. Given set-theoretical foundations, the statement of the [axiom of choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_of_choice) does not translate faithfully (in a way that can be proved) to type-theoretic foundations. In Type theory, we introduce the [type-theoretic axiom of choice](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/type+theoretic+axiom+of+choice), which is provable, unlike the set-theoretic counterpart, which is a stated axiom.

### Function extensionality

More concretely, we pit MLTT against Homotopy Type Theory in its expressiveness. For this, we use the canonical examples of function extensionality, univalence, and the dependent Yoneda lemma. 

In MLTT, to prove function extensionality, one needs a notion of extensional types and, in particular, extensional equality/identity. This is given by the notion of identity types on function types. It is shown [here](https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/bitstream/handle/1810/254394/Polynomials%20and%20Models%20of%20Type%20Theory%20-%20Tamara%20von%20Glehn.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y) that under certain models of Dependent Type Theory, function extensionality fails. In HoTT, it holds due to univalence.

### Univalence

Here we pit STLC against HoTT. Well, this is not a fair fight, but it proves our argument. We cannot prove Univalence in STLC. This is easy to see. HoTT is basically the poster child of univalence.

### Dependent Yoneda Lemma.

For this, we pit vanilla Dependent Type Theory (MLTT) against HoTT as expressed using Cubical Types. We can see where this is going: we can prove the Dependent Yoneda Lemma in HoTT with univalence, but we can't in MLTT. This is left as an exercise for the reader.[^5]

### Invisible Mathematics

In his [talk](https://math.andrej.com/2023/02/13/formalizing-invisible-mathematics/), Andrej discusses how the process of formalizing mathematics within any foundation surfaces a layer of mathematics that is often implicit in natural-language mathematics. This is one aspect of the mismatch between type theory (a chosen foundation of mathematics) and the mathematics in “our heads”. Some foundations can suitably capture this layer while others can’t.  
He also alludes to the fact that type theory is not the final language to be used to formalize mathematics.


# Mathematics

### What is Mathematics?

*Do you know math?*  
*I did the math ...*  
*Show me the math.*  
*What does the math say?*  
*The math says so; therefore it must be right.*  
*The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics.*  
*They won the mathematics competition.*  
*Mathematicians are strategic assets for national security.*  
*Mathematics is what mathematicians do.*  
*It is math about math.*  
*They used math to calculate the size of the Earth.*  
*Is math invented or discovered?*

<p style="text-align:right;">Statements I’ve come across in the mathematics information ecology</p>
<p style="text-align:right;">(as a mathematics enthusiast)</p>

A question we’ve been dodging in all of this is that of the nature of mathematics. What is Mathematics? One reason formalizing mathematics is alluring is that it gives a way to answer this very question, since a formalist might point to the “program/file”  and say that mathematics is that file/program. This is not convincing to us intuitively (but we know that math is often counter-intuitive). The question remains, even if we point to the formalized entities.

### Mathematics as a system of being

*It is through the relationship between people (beings) mediated by language (mathematics) that meaning and being are realized.*

Much of mathematics is for knowledge transfer between two minds; the systems of rules and etiquette around mathematics serve this purpose. It is, in a word, intersubjective. There needs to be a sync between the people interacting, and one way to do this is to have a shared rule set. This gets explicit when we introduce formal mathematics, an answer to the question: “How do we communicate mathematics to computers?” You might already think that your desk calculator or your calculator app understands mathematics, and in a sense it does. But, in a deeper sense, for instance, in verifying the correctness of general mathematical statements, the calculator does not. It’ll help you calculate, but it won’t help you *reason* or verify that your reasoning is sound.[^6]

What do the mathematical constructions being communicated represent? Let’s take the basic example of natural numbers. We can use them to perform arithmetic, although one can argue that the operations on natural numbers (as a Set) are central. This naturally brings us to the notion of abstract algebra, particularly the concept of [groups](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group). When one mathematician sends a group construction to another mathematician, the two share meaning. Meaning is central to being human. By sharing language, we get to make sense of the world collectively.

One question that comes with the advent of proof assistants is: does the intersubjectivity that is central to mathematics practice remain? And our answer is yes. Communication of concepts now has an additional layer of context and correctness such that mathematicians don’t need to “hold” a lot in working memory so as to understand the intricacies of a proof. It also opens the door for wider collaboration, as many proponents of formalized mathematics have argued. This is collective sense-making exemplified.

### Category Theory semi-formal sketches (Some diagrams)

![][image3]


The diagram above is a sketch of our view of the relationship between mathematics and itself, in the context of additional theorems and proofs. It also shows the relationship between mathematics and various type theories. In it, the maps between mathematics show how “new mathematics” has to be integrated with “old mathematics”. For instance, A new theorem is usually proved using constructions from established mathematics. It is from the old that the new can be formed, and it is in the old that the new can find ground. It also shows a correspondence between Math and a Type Theory  (T.T) where different type theories can be used to formalize the same Math. It also illustrates the question: Can a Type theory be extended to create a new type theory? The answer to this seems obvious, but we haven’t checked.

## ![][image4]

This diagram illustrates how Cat (a category) is “operationalized” by a Type Theory. I.e it gives a language for constructing the objects and morphisms of a category. The [industry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/relationship+between+type+theory+and+category+theory) phrase is “one may view type theory as a formal syntactic language or calculus for category theory; conversely, one may think of category theory as providing semantics for type theory”. The F stands for formalization, and the R stands for: Is this Type relevant to math? This is, in a sense, the main subject of our study. What is the difference between the Relevance map and the Formalization map?

### Does formalization Crystallize Mathematical thought?

Given that mathematics can be thought of as a mode of being, does concretizing it in a computational substrate lead to this loss of fluidity? We do not have an answer yet.

# Conjecture 0

We state our argument in a semi-formal way. This is for clarity of the object of our research efforts.

## Statement

By showing how a type theory can fail in expressing a mathematical concept we might hold to be relevant, we open the door to posit the following conjecture:

“There is always a gap between the semantics of a type theory and Mathematics as we do it”

This is a hard conjecture to prove, as it requires us to establish this gap across all possible type theories. To do this, we explore the fact that type theories are internal logics of particular categories. [NLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/type+theory#CategoricalSemantics): “One way to look at type theory, from the point of view of a category theorist, is as a syntax for describing the construction of objects and morphisms in a category. The question then becomes one of category theory: the relationship between category theory and mathematics”.

Mathematical practice is not exhausted by any fixed effective type theory, because it includes the capacity to reason about theories externally, adopt reflection principles, introduce new forms of construction, and revise its representational resources in response to previously encountered limitations.

A lot of work is needed even to make this a provable claim. There is also a lot of research into formal foundations of reasoning and mathematics we can look into.

### Lemma

“There is a gap between category theory and mathematics as we do it”[^7]

Both category theorists and mathematicians have studied the question. A notable example is Lawvere’s [The Category of Categories as a Foundation for Mathematics](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-99902-4_1).

### The Elephant in the room

Gödel’s incompleteness [theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/incompleteness+theorem) can be seen as a proof of the above claim. If we take a categorical foundation of maths to be an axiomatic system, then by Gödel, there are mathematical statements that can be stated by the foundations but cannot be proved in the foundations.

Citing Gödel and calling it doesn’t quite give us a lot to work with. I.e., it doesn’t give us more insight into how any type system will fall short of formalizing all of mathematics and, crucially, why that is true.

Tarski’s own [undefinability theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarski%27s_undefinability_theorem) establishes that the limitation of a formal system is also in its semantics: a sufficiently expressive consistent theory cannot contain an adequate truth predicate for all its own sentences.

Lawvere reveals the shared categorical mechanism behind these results, showing that sufficiently comprehensive self-representation forces fixed points and therefore conflicts with fixed-point-free operations such as negation. Joyal’s categorical proof realizes this mechanism inside arithmetic universes by internalizing syntax, constructing a categorical Gödel proposition, and showing that completeness would collapse the universe into triviality.

Feferman interprets this not as a removable defect of one formalism but as evidence for the “in principle inexhaustibility” of mathematics: once we accept a theory, we can reason about it externally and adopt new axioms or reflection principles that it cannot justify internally.

The precise claim, therefore, is not that every type theory fails to formulate some fixed totality called “all of mathematics,” but that no fixed, consistent, effective, and arithmetically adequate type theory is closed under all mathematically warranted reflection about itself; strengthening the theory can repair one boundary, but only by creating a new external standpoint and, with it, a new boundary.
